questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: 'Just because something can be done does not mean it should be done' expresses the principle of:
questions.rationale: Stewardship: humans have limited dominion and must respect the intrinsic ends of life, avoiding the fallacy of the technological imperative.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Principle of stewardship (PDF p. 60)
questions.quote: simply because something can be done does not necessarily mean that it should be done

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: Proper disposal of used PPE, needles and specimen kits is an example of which stewardship?
questions.rationale: Biomedical stewardship is care in proper disposal of contaminated secretions, equipment and waste.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Biomedical stewardship (PDF p. 64)
questions.quote: Biomedical stewardship is reflected in the utmost care in proper disposal of contaminated body secretions

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A nurse leader uses mentors and coaches to keep improving her skills. This is:
questions.rationale: Personal stewardship (of self) involves lifelong learning with mentors and coaches.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Personal stewardship (PDF p. 62)
questions.quote: nurse leaders or stewards need the use of mentors and personal coaches

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Amputating a gangrenous foot to save the patient's life is justified by the principle of:
questions.rationale: Under totality, a part of the body may be sacrificed for the good of the whole person.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Principle of totality (PDF p. 65)
questions.quote: a part of the human body may be sacrificed if that sacrifice means continued survival for the person

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which procedure fails to meet the principle of totality?
questions.rationale: Removing a healthy organ for non-therapeutic reasons (e.g., to avoid having a child, vanity) is not justified by totality.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Totality: non-justifiable (PDF p. 65)
questions.quote: Removal of the uterus (hysterectomy) because you don't want to have a child

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which is a condition for applying the principle of totality?
questions.rationale: Conditions: the diseased part threatens the whole, there is no other way, and the harm avoided is proportionate.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Conditions for totality (PDF p. 65)
questions.quote: that there is no other way than taking the indicated action against it

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Before the incision is closed, the OR nurse's ethical duty to protect the patient's body means ensuring:
questions.rationale: Before suturing, all materials are counted and controlled so nothing remains in the patient's body.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Nurses in surgery (PDF p. 67)
questions.quote: ensuring that nothing remains in the patient's body

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which action best preserves dignity of an anesthetized patient in the OR?
questions.rationale: Conversation in the OR should be professional, mindful of what is said whether the patient is awake or not.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Preserve patient's dignity (PDF p. 67)
questions.quote: it should be done professionally and considering what is said now, whether the patient is awake or not

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which perioperative action helps prevent surgical site infection?
options: Limit people moving in the OR
questions.rationale: Preventing postoperative infection includes minimizing the number of people and their movement in the OR.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Nurses in surgery (PDF p. 67)
questions.quote: preventing postoperative infections by minimizing the number of people

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: For elderly surgical patients, the OR nurse must be especially vigilant to prevent:
questions.rationale: Protecting the patient's body includes preventing hypothermia, especially in elderly patients.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Nurses in surgery (PDF p. 66)
questions.quote: Responsibility also means preventing hypothermia, especially in the care of elderly patients.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which living donation is ethically acceptable only in very rare cases?
questions.rationale: Donating a nonpaired, nonrenewable organ like the heart means the donor's death.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Issues in organ donation (PDF p. 69)
questions.quote: The donation of a nonpaired, nonrenewable organ such as the heart or the entire liver from a living donor spells death for the donor.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A family pressures a reluctant sibling to donate a kidney. The nurse recognizes this as:
questions.rationale: Donor autonomy must be respected; pressuring or 'blackmailing' donors is unethical and providers should guard against it.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Ethics of the recipient (PDF p. 69)
questions.quote: While such pressure is humanly understandable, it is unethical, and health care providers should guard against it.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Why should a potential cadaver donor be declared dead by a physician other than the recipient's?
questions.rationale: A separate physician avoids the reality and appearance of a conflict of loyalties.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Ethics of the health care team (PDF p. 71)
questions.quote: the donor must be declared dead by at least one physician other than the physician of the recipient

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A dying patient is a potential organ donor. Until death, the team should:
questions.rationale: The donor continues to get usual care so the team is not tempted to hasten death for organs.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Ethics of the health care team (PDF p. 71)
questions.quote: the physician should continue to give the donor the same care as usual

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A major ethical concern with selling organs is:
questions.rationale: Organ sale risks exploiting the poor and distributing organs by ability to pay rather than need.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Selling organs (PDF p. 70)
questions.quote: The first problem that might, result from widespread sale Of organs involves the exploitation Of the poor

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A treatment that offers reasonable hope of benefit without excessive pain or cost is:
questions.rationale: Ordinary (proportionate) means offer reasonable hope of benefit without excessive burden and are morally obligatory.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Ordinary and extraordinary means (PDF p. 73)

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A terminally ill patient declines a costly, painful treatment with little hope of benefit. Ethically, this treatment is:
questions.rationale: Disproportionate means (no reasonable hope of benefit or excessive burden) may be foregone.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Ordinary and extraordinary means (PDF p. 73)
questions.quote: a person may forego extraordinary or disproportionate means of preserving life

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A patient dying of advanced cancer develops early-stage kidney disease. Is she obliged to treat it?
questions.rationale: Those dying of one illness have no obligation to accept treatment for a second, less advanced life-threatening one.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Extraordinary treatment (PDF p. 74)
questions.quote: Those who are dying of one illness have no obligation to accept treatment for a second life-threatening one
